subject: Hindu Religious Education

source.title: Primary School Education Curriculum Design — Hindu Religious Education, Grade 6 (Revised 2024)
source.notes: Read directly from grade-6-curriculum-desings/GRADE-6-HRE-Curriculum-Designs.pdf via the Read tool (no pages param), full text, all 8 strands / 11 sub-strands / 90 lessons. Learning Area allocation: 3 lessons/week at Upper Primary (Religious Education line item). Essence statement frames Grade 6 HRE as a four-faith rotation (Sanatan/Vedic, Jainism, Buddhism, Sikhism) with this grade leaning heavily on Buddhist and Sikh content specifically, unlike the broader four-faith spread seen in some sub-strands of the Grade 7/8/9 designs.

subStrands.name: 1.1 Creation in Buddh and Sikh Faiths
specificLearningOutcomes: identify the concepts of creation from Buddh and Sikhi faiths for familiarisation
display concepts of creation for deeper understanding
appreciate different concepts of creation for social awareness
keyInquiryQuestions: Why is it important to know creation concepts in Buddh and Sikh faiths?
How does the concept of creation help one appreciate Paramatma?
learningExperiences: mention the concept of creation from Buddhism and Sikhism
discuss with peers the different creation concepts
watch a video on discourse by a spiritual teacher
ask their elders/parents questions on the different concepts of creation
prepare a skit from a Scriptural story and perform as a group activity
visit places of worship accompanied by parents/guardian/teacher
inquire more about the concepts of creation in Buddh and Sikh faiths
search and report on different creation concepts using search engines/Scriptures/library/resource person
linkedLearningAreas: Creative Arts — skills of using digital devices while watching a video on discourse by a spiritual teacher
scopeNotes: Content pool is conceptual (Buddhist and Sikh creation concepts), not a fixed enumerated list of named items — the design gives no closed set of terms here, unlike 1.2's seven named animals/birds.
subStrands.assessmentSignal: Rubric distinguishes correctly-identifying-with-meanings vs. correctly-identifying vs. only-when-prompted vs. cannot-identify-even-when-prompted for the Buddhism/Sikhism creation concepts — depth of explanation, not just recall, is explicitly rewarded.

subStrands.name: 1.2 Gifts of Nature
specificLearningOutcomes: identify the selected seven birds and animals used in the four faiths
match birds and animals in the four faiths with their importance
appreciate the importance of specific birds and animals according to the four faiths
keyInquiryQuestions: How do specific birds and animals give symbolic significance in different faiths?
How do Scriptural stories show interdependence of nature and humans?
learningExperiences: give names of selected birds and animals from the four faiths
discuss with peers the religious importance of selected animals and birds
prepare a skit from a Scriptural story and perform it as a group activity
draw animals and birds of religious importance using digital devices
take videos and photos of birds and animals and identify the ones of religious importance
listen to radio lessons and stories related to birds and animals of religious importance/watch videos
participate in a charity walk to raise funds to preserve the environment
visit the temple/museum to observe pictures/murals/sculptures of birds and animals
assist learners with special needs as per their abilities through peer teaching importance of birds and animals that are considered sacred
engage in discussions with peers to highlight symbolic significance of birds and animals of religious importance as related to Enlightened Beings
linkedLearningAreas: Agriculture & Nutrition — skills of classifying and giving names to birds and animals
Creative Arts — skills of using digital devices and drawing animals and birds of religious importance
scopeNotes: The design names exactly 7 selected animals/birds: cow, peacock, horse, elephant, hawk, Garur, lion — this is a closed, hard-floor list per the mining guide, not a sampling menu.

Assessment rubric's top band explicitly requires identifying all 7 and explaining their significance, and separately requires matching all 7 to their importance — both identify and match are independently assessed abilities.
subStrands.assessmentSignal: Four-tier rubric on both 'identify the 7' and 'match the 7 to importance': all 7 with explanation > all 7 correctly > 4-6 correctly > fewer than 4 — so a skill's content pool must genuinely support all 7 distinctly, not treat them interchangeably.

subStrands.name: 2.1 Enlightened Beings and Social Welfare
specificLearningOutcomes: identify key events from the lives of the selected Enlightened beings for social welfare
classify the contributions of the Enlightened Beings for inspiration
appreciate the teachings of the Enlightened Beings to enhance social harmony
keyInquiryQuestions: How does the teaching of the Enlightened Beings contribute to social welfare?
learningExperiences: read the life histories of the selected Enlightened Beings using digital devices, resource persons and other relevant sources
discuss with parents/guardian/teacher to gain knowledge on Enlightened Beings
listen to stories of Enlightened Beings using Scriptures/a resource person/audio-visual device
research and write essays on the lives of Enlightened Beings
role-play/perform skits based on the key events from the lives of Enlightened Beings
assist learners with special needs as per their abilities
draw sketches of Enlightened Beings using digital devices/drawing books
watch animated films on Enlightened Beings using digital devices
linkedLearningAreas: Creative Arts — skills of using digital devices/drawing books to draw sketches of Enlightened Beings
Science and Technology — skills of using digital devices to watch animated films
scopeNotes: The design's bullet list renders as 3 lines — Raja Ram Mohan Rai, Atma Ram Ji Sarriputa, Sri Guru Hargobind Sahib ji — but the rubric's 'four selected Enlightened Beings' language, combined with this strand's grade-wide four-faith rotation pattern (Sanatan/Vedic, Jain, Buddhist, Sikh — one per faith elsewhere in this design), strongly indicates the middle line is two run-together names, not one: 'Atma Ram Ji' (the Jain monk and reformer Acharya Vijayanand Suri, popularly known as Atmaramji Maharaj, 1837-1896) and 'Sariputta' (the Buddhist chief disciple of Gautama Buddha, renowned for wisdom). A PDF line-break/bullet-separator likely did not survive extraction between these two names.

Resolved on that basis as 4 Enlightened Beings, one per faith: Raja Ram Mohan Rai (Sanatan/Vedic — Brahmo Samaj founder, campaigned against Sati), Atma Ram Ji / Acharya Vijayanand Suri (Jain — sent a Jain philosophy essay to the 1893 World's Parliament of Religions in Chicago, since Jain monastic vows forbid sea travel), Sariputta (Buddhist — the Buddha's chief disciple, called 'General of the Dharma' for his wisdom), and Sri Guru Hargobind Sahib ji (Sikh — introduced Miri-Piri, built the Akal Takht). This reading matches the rubric's headline count and the strand's own four-faith structure better than treating the pool as 3, though it remains a curatorial inference rather than a verbatim-confirmed 4th bullet line.
subStrands.assessmentSignal: Rubric (as written, referencing 'four') rewards identifying key events + classifying contributions for each Enlightened Being, elaborately/with modelling at the top band — down to fewer than two at the bottom band.

subStrands.name: 3.1 Scriptures and Moral Values
specificLearningOutcomes: identify the teachings of Scriptures that enhance moral values for familiarisation
interpret the teachings of Scriptures to foster social harmony
appreciate teaching of scriptures for enhancing moral values
keyInquiryQuestions: How do Scriptural stories contribute to instilling moral values?
How can we apply teachings of scriptures to instilling moral values?
learningExperiences: read scriptures that enhance moral values, in groups
listen to stories/resource persons/audio-visual devices to know about the role of the Scriptures
share stories from Scriptures that explain their roles as carriers of moral values
recite mantras from Scriptures based on their roles to instil moral values
use search engines to identify the Scriptural stories that enhance moral values in the community
hold discussions on the role of Scriptures
assist learners with special needs as per their abilities through peer teaching lessons drawn from the Scriptural stories
linkedLearningAreas: Social Studies — skills of socialising and sharing stories from Scriptures
Creative Arts — skills of using audio-visual devices to listen to stories/resource persons
scopeNotes: The design names exactly 4 selected Scriptures: Bhagwad Gita, Uttradhayaan (Ch. 13-18), Sutta Pitaka, Sri Guru Granth Sahib ji — this is a closed, hard-floor list of 4, matching the rubric's own 'four selected Scriptures' language (unlike 2.1, this sub-strand's list and rubric count agree).
subStrands.assessmentSignal: Rubric explicitly requires identifying the teachings of all 4 selected Scriptures at the top two bands, dropping to 3 then fewer than 2 at lower bands — separately assesses interpreting the teachings (with/without assistance).

subStrands.name: 4.1 Basic Chants/Mantras as per Buddhism
specificLearningOutcomes: identify basic chants/the mantras of paying homage to the Buddha for spiritual nourishment
describe the importance of tisarana (taking refuge in triple gem) for spiritual growth
appreciate pancha sila (five precepts) for moral development
keyInquiryQuestions: How is recitation of chants/mantras important in Buddhist occasions?
learningExperiences: mention basic chants/mantras according to the Buddha faith
discuss with peers how chanting these mantras helps one develop moral values and spiritual growth
recite the 3 basic chants of Buddhist practice with aid of digital devices
watch animated short story on importance of tisarana using digital devices
listen to a resource person to guide in moral education through pancha sila mantra
visit a Buddhist vihaar to understand the application of these mantras in real life
assist learners with special needs as per their abilities through peer teaching the religious practices carried out in a place of worship
write a composition on how to apply pancha sila in real life
linkedLearningAreas: English — skills of writing a composition on how to apply pancha sila in real life
Creative Arts — skills of using digital devices to recite the 3 basic chants
scopeNotes: The design names exactly 3 basic chants/practices: paying homage (to the Buddha), tisarana (taking refuge in the triple gem), and pancha sila (the five precepts) — explicitly called 'the 3 basic chants of Buddhist practice' in the learning experiences, so this is a closed 3-item pool.
subStrands.assessmentSignal: Three separate rubric rows — one per named chant/practice (paying-homage chants, tisarana, Buddhist Vihaar practices/ceremonies is actually 4.2's row; here rows are paying-homage chants and tisarana specifically) — each independently graded from 'correctly + recites them'/'with examples' down to 'struggles even when prompted'.

subStrands.name: 4.2 Buddhist Vihaars in Africa
specificLearningOutcomes: identify the practices and ceremonies held in Buddhist Vihaar for social awareness
distinguish the significance of the features in a Buddhist Vihaar from other symbols for familiarisation
appreciate the value of Buddhist Vihaar in Africa for moral and spiritual wellness
keyInquiryQuestions: Why is it important to visit a place of worship?
What is the importance of the features found in a Buddhist temple?
learningExperiences: name practices and ceremonies held in a Buddhist Vihaar
collect pictures of Buddhist Vihaar in Africa from magazines/newspapers/digital devices
discuss with peers the different features of Buddhist Vihaar
create a montage using photos from the places of worship
visit places of worship to witness activities carried out at different times
use digital devices to locate the Buddhist Vihaar in Kenya
assist learners with special needs as per their abilities through peer teaching draw and colour the Buddhist Vihaar
visit a Buddhist Vihaar to witness ceremonies, architecture and other important features
linkedLearningAreas: Creative Arts — skills of creating a montage using photos, and drawing/colouring the Buddhist Vihaar
scopeNotes: Content is architectural/ceremonial-practice based (features, ceremonies, locating Vihaars in Kenya specifically) rather than a fixed named list — no closed enumeration of individual features is given in the source text beyond 'practices and ceremonies' and 'features' generically.
subStrands.assessmentSignal: Rubric rewards identifying practices/ceremonies held in a Buddhist Vihaar 'correctly with examples' at the top band down to 'struggles even when prompted' at the bottom.

subStrands.name: 5.1 Managing Resources
specificLearningOutcomes: classify the types of resources relevant in their life for harmonious living
explain correct uses of various resources for better living
demonstrate appropriate use of resources for sustainable development
develop a desire to use and manage resources prudently for sustainable development
keyInquiryQuestions: How can we take care of resources in school and community?
Why is it important for an individual to take care of resources?
How is technology useful in managing resources prudently?
learningExperiences: name different types of resources
research and classify different types of commonly used resources
compare and adopt various strategies from other countries to manage resources
discuss with peers appropriate use of resources
plan for and share resources with the less fortunate in society
download and use time management applications from digital devices
initiate campaign with peers to motivate peers to be punctual in all school activities
create a hypothetical budget with priority items to be purchased within the available funds
design posters indicating switching off the electric appliances/turning off the taps after use at school/home/community centres
watch videos on managing resources in an appropriate manner
model the managing of resources prudently for sustainable development
visit a home for the less fortunate to appreciate the value of responsible use of food
linkedLearningAreas: Creative Arts — skills of designing posters indicating switching off electric appliances/turning off taps
scopeNotes: The design names exactly 4 resource types: natural, financial, man-made, time — a closed 4-item pool matching the rubric's own 'four types of resources' language.
subStrands.assessmentSignal: Rubric separately grades (a) demonstrating appropriate use of resources for sustainable development and (b) classifying all 4 resource types — top band for (b) requires all 4 with details, dropping to 3 then not-more-than-2 at lower bands.

subStrands.name: 6.1 Asanas
specificLearningOutcomes: describe the types of Pranayam and Asanas for familiarisation
practise Pranayam and Asanas for physical wellbeing
acknowledge the importance of Pranayam and Asanas for healthy living
keyInquiryQuestions: Why are Asanas important in Yoga?
What is the importance of Pranayam in life?
learningExperiences: brainstorm about the different types of Pranayams and Asanas
collect pictures from magazines, newspapers/digital platforms on Pranayams and Asanas
visit and participate in the celebration of International Yoga Day
practise the Asanas with peers under the supervision of a resource person
practice the breathing exercises of Pranaayam using digital device
perform Pranayams correctly under the supervision of a resource person
make a journal to record their Yoga practice and changes observed in themselves
create a Yoga guidance video using digital devices
demonstrate correct postures of Asanas
linkedLearningAreas: Creative Arts — skills of using digital devices to make a journal/video and demonstrate postures
scopeNotes: The design names exactly 3 Pranayam (breathing exercise) types: Bhramari (humming bee breath), Sheetali Pranayaam (cooling breath), Sheet kari Pranayaam (hissing breath).
The design names exactly 3 Asanas (physical postures): Dhanur Asan, Vajra asan, Chakra chalan asan.
Together this is a closed 6-item pool (3 Pranayams + 3 Asanas), each with a distinct named technique/breath style.
subStrands.assessmentSignal: Rubric grades describing the types of Pranayam and Asanas from 'correctly and recites/demonstrates them' down to 'struggles even when prompted' — description depth (not just naming) is rewarded at the top band.

subStrands.name: 6.2 Communal Aspect of Yoga
specificLearningOutcomes: explain the benefits of environmental protection for communal wellness
assess improvements they observed in themselves over a specific period for self-evaluation
illustrate ways of protecting the environment for sustainable development
embrace Yoga for harmonious living
keyInquiryQuestions: How are the different aspects of Yoga beneficial to society?
How do Yoga and meditation influence one's life?
learningExperiences: research with the aid of a digital device/resource person, case studies of communities that have benefited from environmental conservation
participate in cleaning the school compound campaign
organise a tree planting drive in school
make posters on how to conserve the environment and display in the school compound and in the community centres
sensitise the school community on negative effects of noise and air pollution
participate in communal Yoga to practise meditation and exercises
compose/sing/recite songs/poems on peace, in groups
work with the guidance and counselling teacher in school to address some critical issues encountered by learners
assist learners with special needs as per their abilities through peer teaching basic meditation in Yoga
linkedLearningAreas: Agriculture & Nutrition — skills of tree planting when organising a tree planting drive
scopeNotes: The design names 3 communal-aspect themes: enhanced wellness, harmonious living, environmental protection — a closed 3-item pool, each explicitly listed as a sub-strand focus term.
subStrands.assessmentSignal: Rubric separately grades (a) explaining the benefits of environmental protection (with details/examples down to major mix-ups) and (b) illustrating ways of protecting the environment (with examples down to challenges even when prompted).

subStrands.name: 7.1 Virtues and Principles of Dharma in Buddhism
specificLearningOutcomes: describe the primary virtues from Buddhist stories for righteousness
interpret the relevance of key virtues for righteousness from Buddhist stories in their life
uphold the Principles of Dharma in building one's character for citizenship
keyInquiryQuestions: Why is it important to observe virtues for righteousness?
How can one implement Principles of Dharma in daily life?
How can Principles of Dharma be applied in classroom situations?
learningExperiences: watch discourses and narrate relevant stories on Principles of Dharma in Buddhism
perform skits based on the narrated stories
download information on virtues for righteousness using digital devices and discuss in groups
visit a Buddhist Vihaar accompanied by parents/guardians to learn Principles of Dharma
implement Principles of Dharma in class during activities appropriately
dramatise Scriptural stories based on the Principles of Dharma
linkedLearningAreas: Creative Arts — skills of dramatising Scriptural stories
scopeNotes: Content is Buddhist-story-based virtues in general (based on Scriptural stories per the sub-strand's own subtitle) — the source text does not enumerate a fixed closed list of named virtues here, unlike sub-strands with explicit bulleted item lists (e.g. 1.2, 3.1).

The shipped skill fills this open sub-strand with the ten Paramitas (perfections) — Dana, Sila, Nekkhamma, Panna, Viriya, Khanti, Sacca, Adhitthana, Metta, Upekkha — the standard, well-documented Theravada Buddhist virtue framework that Jataka tales are traditionally organised around (e.g. Prince Vessantara's story illustrating Dana). This is a curatorial choice to give the open sub-strand concrete, accurate content, not a verbatim KICD-text enumeration.
subStrands.assessmentSignal: Rubric separately grades (a) describing primary virtues from Buddhist stories and (b) interpreting the relevance of key virtues in the learner's own life, each on the standard 4-tier scale from 'with illustrations/examples' down to 'challenges even when prompted'.

subStrands.name: 8.1 Utsavs from Other Faiths
specificLearningOutcomes: state the significance of celebrating the festivals for posterity
participate in festivals for social cohesion and harmony
nurture the value of celebrating festivals towards spiritual growth and social harmony
recognise special days of the month as per Indian traditional calendar for spirituality and social harmony
keyInquiryQuestions: Why do we celebrate festivals?
How do festivals enhance social harmony?
Why are festivals that fall on Purnima and Amavasya considered more auspicious?
learningExperiences: listen to stories/narrate stories about the significance of celebrating festivals
watch videos on religious festivals observed in Christian and Islamic faiths
take active part in the celebration of festivals and write reports on how the festivals are celebrated
sing Christmas carols and Surahs in relation to the festivals
do charity work at homes of children and the elderly, visit schools of children with special needs for inclusive celebrations
assist learners with special needs to safely participate during group activities
perform skits based on the festivals
listen to a resource person on the significance of special days of month as per the four faiths
download the Indian traditional calendar to show dates of these special days
use search engines to understand different phases of the moon
linkedLearningAreas: Creative Arts — skill of singing Christmas carols and Surahs
scopeNotes: The design names 2 non-Hindu festivals for cross-faith awareness: Christmas, Eid-ul-Fitr.

The design names 3 Indian traditional calendar special days: Sankranti, Amavasya (No Moon Day), Purnima (Full Moon Day) — explicitly tied to 'in four faiths', i.e. these calendar days are observed across all four faiths this design covers.
Together this is a closed 5-item pool (2 cross-faith festivals + 3 calendar special days).
subStrands.assessmentSignal: Rubric grades (a) stating the significance of celebrating the festivals (with examples down to challenges even when motivated) and (b) participating in festivals (encourages peers down to only-when-motivated).

appendixNotes: The Appendix (List of Assessment Methods, Learning Resources and Non-Formal Activities) names 'Panchmahabhoot' as a Strand-1 (Creation) resource/topic keyword not otherwise spelled out in the strand's own body text (which stays at the conceptual level for 1.1). This is a suggested-resource-table term, not a further enumerated content item with its own learning outcomes — noted here for completeness per the mining guide, not treated as an additional hard-floor content pool.
CSL (Community Service Learning) at Upper Primary is hosted in Social Studies, not HRE itself, and is a once-annual cross-curricular activity — not a source of HRE-specific skill content.
